stops.name: The six-dot cell complete, twelve reduced to six (1824)
stops.campa: At fifteen the work is done. He has folded the twelve dots into six: two columns of three, a single cell the fingertip covers at one touch and reads in one instant. Sixty-three combinations, and from them a whole language of letters, accents, punctuation, all of it. He carries it to his friends and runs their fingers across it, and it is swift, swift as no blind hand has ever read before. The soldier's cipher for sounds in the dark has become, in a blind boy's hands, an alphabet for the whole mind. It is the invention entire, and it will not change again.

stops.name: The Institute, pupil becomes teacher (répétiteur, 1828; professor, 1833)
stops.campa: The brilliant pupil is kept on: first répétiteur at nineteen, then, by 1833, full professor of the Institute. He teaches grammar, geometry, algebra, history: to the blind, in his own dots, though the administration will not yet own the system. The children love him; he is gentle, exact, unhurried, and he is one of them. In the classrooms of the rue Saint-Victor the new alphabet spreads hand to hand among the pupils faster than any decree can travel. The invention lives already, underground, in the fingers of the children he teaches.

stops.name: The published book, Procédé pour écrire les paroles, la musique et le plain-chant (1829)
stops.campa: He publishes his method: 'A Process for Writing Words, Music, and Plainchant by Means of Dots, for the Use of the Blind and Arranged for Them.' The irony is bitter and exact: the book that announces the dots is printed in Haüy's old raised letters, the only script the Institute will sanction. Within its covers stands the full system: the alphabet, and already music, for the organist has bent his own art to the finger. In 1837 he will issue it again, cleaner, casting out the last dashes. The word is now, for the first time, a thing the blind may both read and write.

stops.name: Church of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, the blind organist (1834–1839)
stops.campa: From 1834 he holds the organ of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, a great old church of the Marais. The blind master climbs to the loft and takes the manuals, and the vast instrument answers his hands: plainchant, fugue, the Mass carried on stops he cannot see but knows by touch as intimately as his own alphabet. Parisians below hear only the music; they do not know the player is sightless, nor that his fingers, when they leave the keys, read and write a script the seeing world has yet to grant. He is master of two keyboards, the organ and the cell.

stops.name: The raphigraphe, letters of dots for sighted eyes (New Method, 1839)
stops.campa: He reaches across the wall between the blind and the seeing. In his 'New Method for Representing by Dots the Form of Letters,' with the raphigraphe device, a blind hand can punch out ordinary Roman letters, built entirely of dots, that a sighted reader can read with the eye. It is his answer to the loneliness of the invention: not only that the blind should read among themselves, but that they should write to the whole world, and be answered. A letter home to Coupvray, in the boy's own hand, that his seeing mother can read: this is what the dots are for.

stops.name: Church of Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, the later organ loft
stops.campa: In his later years he serves the organ of Saint-Vincent-de-Paul as well, one of several Paris churches that give the blind master their manuals. The faith received at the Coupvray font is here at its center; he plays the Mass, the offices, the great feasts, week upon week, a devout man in the loft above the incense. The cough has begun by now, the fever that will not lift; but at the organ he is whole. Music and religion are, for Louis Braille, the two rooms of one house, and the church is where the alphabet-maker goes to rest his hands upon something larger than himself.

stops.name: The sighted director: Pierre-Armand Dufau takes the Institute (1840)
stops.campa: The kindly director Pignier, who had let the dots quietly live, is forced out, and Pierre-Armand Dufau takes his chair. Dufau is sighted, ambitious, and frightened: an alphabet only the blind can read makes the blind independent of their seeing keepers, and independent of him. He resolves to stamp it out and restore the old raised letters that keep the blind forever needing a sighted hand. The invention, like every true thing the world is not ready for, meets its persecutor. The books that hold the code are marked for the fire.

stops.name: The burning, the books of dots in the courtyard fire
stops.campa: Dufau makes a bonfire in the rear courtyard and burns them: every volume in Louis's code, hand-copied and printed, the whole library and the labour of years. He seizes the slates and styli too, so no dot may be written again. It is the corpus's oldest story, the true thing set alight by the frightened powerful. But the pupils will not be unmade. Behind his back, denied slates, they write the forbidden dots with knitting needles and forks and nails, keep secret diaries, pass messages in the dark, and the alphabet the flames were meant to kill goes on being written in the very house that burned it.

stops.name: Boulevard des Invalides: the new house, and the turning (1844)
stops.campa: The Institute moves to a sound new building on the boulevard des Invalides, and at its solemn inauguration the persecutor is turned. Prompted by his assistant Joseph Guadet, Dufau lets a blind girl read aloud from a page she has never seen, transcribed in Louis's dots before the assembled dignitaries, and then read it flawlessly. The hall is astonished. The point is made in the only language power understands: the thing works, and nothing can be done. Dufau, who burned the books, becomes their champion. The invention has survived its fire.

stops.name: The consumption, the teacher forced to lay down his post
stops.campa: The tuberculosis he first breathed in the damp of the rue Saint-Victor has never left him; through his thirties it climbs. By his early forties the fevers and the blood force him to give up teaching. He withdraws, keeps only a little private instruction and the organ loft, and lives quietly, without bitterness, in the shadow of the illness. He has finished his work and knows it is finished. What he cannot yet know is how the world will use it. He waits, failing, in a serenity his friends will remember all their lives.

stops.name: The sacraments, 'my mission on earth is accomplished' (December 1851)
stops.campa: In mid-December, feeling the end near, he calls a priest and receives the sacraments of his church: the faith of the Coupvray font returning to him whole at the last. The next day he rallies briefly, and to his friend Hippolyte Coltat he speaks with a strange bright calm: he has tasted, he says, all the majesty and power of religion, and he is at peace. He is convinced, he tells him, that his mission on earth is accomplished. He does not mean the alphabet, which the world still scarcely uses; he means his soul. But the sentence will belong to both.
stops.quote: I am convinced my mission on earth is accomplished.
stops.quote_source: Recorded by Hippolyte Coltat; reported in the early biographies of Louis Braille (December 1851)

stops.name: Death at the Institute, Paris: 6 January 1852
stops.campa: On the sixth of January, two days after his forty-third birthday, Louis Braille dies in the infirmary of the Institute on the boulevard des Invalides, among the blind children who are already, in secret, his heirs. He goes quietly, the serenity unbroken. The seeing world takes little notice; the newspapers are thin. Almost no one alive understands that the man who has just died has done more for the reading of the human race than any since Gutenberg. The alphabet lies finished in the fingers of a few hundred pupils, waiting, like a seed under snow.
